'''Claude R. LeBrun''' (born 1956) is an American mathematician who holds the position of Distinguished Professor of Mathematics at [[Stony Brook University]]. Much of his research concerns the [[Glossary of Riemannian and metric geometry|Riemannian geometry]] of 4-manifolds, or related topics in complex and differential geometry.

After enrolling as an undergraduate at [[Rice University]] at age 16,  LeBrun received  his  [[Master of Arts]] in mathematics from [[Rice University|Rice]] in 1977. He then went on to earn his  [[Doctor of Philosophy|D.Phil.]] (Oxford equivalent of a Ph.D.) from the [[University of Oxford]] in 1980, at the age of 23, for a thesis  on complex differential geometry written under the supervision of [[Roger Penrose]].<ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=Claude R. LeBrun|id=11629}}</ref> That same year, he then accepted his first faculty position at Stony Brook.<ref name="sb">[http://www.math.sunysb.edu/html/faculty-rank.shtml Math Department and Institute Faculty - by Rank], Stony Brook University, retrieved 2013-01-30.</ref> 
Although he would eventually go on to spend most  of his career at Stony Brook,  he has also held positions at a number of other institutions, including 
the [[Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques]], the [[Mathematical Sciences Research Institute]], and the [[Institute for Advanced Study]].<ref>[http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/  A Community of Scholars | Institute for Advanced Study, retrieved 2013-05-15.]</ref>

He is the namesake of the [[Lebrun manifold|LeBrun manifold]]s, a family of self-dual manifolds that he discovered in 1989 and that was named after him by [[Michael Atiyah]] and [[Edward Witten]].<ref>{{Citation | last1=Atiyah | first1=Michael | author1-link=Michael Atiyah | last2=Witten | first2=Edward | author2-link=Edward Witten | title=M-theory dynamics on a manifold of G2 holonomy | arxiv=hep-th/0107177 | year=2003 | journal=Advances in Theoretical and Mathematical Physics | issn=1095-0761 | volume=6 | issue=1 | pages=1–106| doi=10.4310/ATMP.2002.v6.n1.a1 | bibcode=2001hep.th....7177A | s2cid=119433129 }}</ref> LeBrun is also known for his work on [[Einstein manifold]]s and the [[Yamabe invariant]]. In particular, he produced examples showing that the [[Converse (logic)#Converse of a theorem|converse]] of the [[Hitchin–Thorpe inequality]] does not hold: there exist infinitely many four-dimensional compact smooth simply connected [[manifold]]s that obey the inequality but do not admit Einstein metrics.

LeBrun was an invited speaker at the 1994 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]].<ref name="sb"/> In 2012, he became a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2013-01-27.</ref> In 2016, a conference in his honor was held at the Centre de Recherches Mathématiques in Montreal.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160114080435/http://www.crm.umontreal.ca/2016/LeBrunFest16/index_e.php/ Conference on Differential Geometry], retrieved 2016-01-14.</ref>
In 2018, he became a Simons Foundation Fellow in Mathematics.<ref>[https://www.simonsfoundation.org/2018/03/23/2018-simons-fellows-in-mathematics-and-theoretical-physics-announced/ Simons Foundation], retrieved 2018-04-28.</ref>
In 2020, he was appointed as Distinguished Professor at the State University of New York.<ref>[https://news.stonybrook.edu/facultystaff/four-sbu-faculty-rise-to-rank-of-suny-distinguished-professor/  Stony Brook University], retrieved 2020-12-10.</ref> In 2025, he became a Simons Foundation Fellow in Mathematics for the second time,<ref>[https://www.simonsfoundation.org/grant/simons-fellows-in-mathematics/?tab=awardees/ Simons Foundation], retrieved 2025-07-21.</ref> while also 
becoming a laureate of the Chaires d'Excellence program of the Fondation Sciences Mathématiques de Paris.<ref>[https://www.sciencesmaths-paris.fr/nos-programmes/les-chaires-fsmp/ Chaires d'Excellence], retrieved 2025-07-21.</ref> In 2026, a conference in his honor <ref>[https://indico.ictp.it/event/11144/ International Conference on Complex and Differential Geomety].</ref> was held at the International Center for Theoretical Physics in Trieste, Italy.
